ops.new: CMS has revised the benchmark methodology repeatedly in response to this problem — adding regional adjustments for agreement periods beginning in 2017, reworking them in the 2018 Pathways to Success rule, and, in the CY2023 Physician Fee Schedule rule, adding a prior-savings adjustment and an administratively set growth factor (the Accountable Care Prospective Trend) to blunt the ratchet effect — but
ops.claim: CMS modified the benchmark 'three times since 2012', most recently Pathways (2018) and 'the 2023 ACO Primary Care Flex Model'
ops.sources: CMS Shared Savings Program final rule (June 2016, regional adjustment); Pathways to Success final rule (Dec 2018); CY2023 PFS final rule (Nov 2022: ACPT and prior savings adjustment from 2024); CMS ACO Primary Care Flex Model page (announced March 2024, began 2025-01-01; a primary care payment model, not a benchmark change)
ops.note: PC Flex is not a benchmark modification and was not a 2023 model; count unsupported.

ops.old: A study published in Health Affairs in 2024 analyzing Medicare spending patterns across 306 hospital referral regions found that regions with above-median primary care physician supply had 11.2% lower total Medicare spending per beneficiary, 18.4% fewer preventable hospital admissions, and 14.7% lower 30-day readmission rates than regions with below-median primary care supply, after controlling for demographic and health status differences.
ops.new: The evidence is strongest on outcomes and quality: Baicker and Chandra (Health Affairs, 2004) found that states with more general practitioners per capita delivered higher-quality care to Medicare beneficiaries at lower spending, while states with more specialists spent more for lower quality; and Basu and colleagues (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2019) found that every 10 additional primary care physicians per 100,000 people was associated with a 51.5-day increase in life expectancy. Supply alone is not a cost-control lever, however — a 2009 Health Affairs analysis found that simply having more primary care physicians did not slow spending growth — which is why payment models that reward primary care for total cost matter.
ops.claim: Health Affairs 2024 study of 306 HRRs: above-median PCP supply -> 11.2% lower spending, 18.4% fewer preventable admissions, 14.7% lower readmissions
ops.sources: Baicker K, Chandra A. Medicare spending, the physician workforce, and beneficiaries' quality of care. Health Affairs 2004;W4-184; Basu S et al. Association of Primary Care Physician Supply With Population Mortality in the United States, 2005-2015. JAMA Intern Med 2019 (Stanford Medicine news, Feb 2019); Goodman DC, Fisher ES et al., 'Would Having More Primary Care Doctors Cut Health Spending Growth?' Health Affairs 2009;28(5):1327
ops.note: No such 2024 study; replaced with real, correctly attributed findings including the contrary evidence.
